key_terms.meaning: Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν; ρ is density in kg/m³, V the mean velocity in m/s, D the pipe diameter in m, μ the dynamic viscosity in Pa·s and ν = μ/ρ the kinematic viscosity in m²/s. It compares inertia force with viscous force.
Flow in smooth parallel layers with no mixing across the pipe; dye stays as one straight thread; Re below the critical value.
Flow with random eddies, cross-mixing and fluctuating velocities; the dye thread breaks into a cloud; Re above the critical value.
The Re band where the dye streak first wavers and then breaks up; in pipe flow it lies roughly between 2000 and 4000, and 2000 is commonly taken as the lower critical value.
For steady laminar flow in a circular pipe, Q = πΔpD⁴/(128μL) and the head loss is h_f = 32μVL/(ρgD²); Q is discharge in m³/s, Δp pressure drop in Pa, L length in m.
In laminar pipe flow u(r) = u_max(1 − r²/R²); u is velocity in m/s at radius r, R the pipe radius in m, so the profile is a paraboloid of revolution.
V = Q/A and u_max = 2V, so the mean velocity is half the centreline velocity.
Dimensionless f in h_f = fLV²/(2gD) = 4f′LV²/(2gD), where f′ is the Fanning friction factor, so f = 4f′.
ε/D, the absolute roughness height ε in m divided by pipe diameter D in m; it decides how much roughness matters in turbulent flow.
1/√f = −2 log₁₀(ε/(3.7D) + 2.51/(Re√f)); it fits the Moody diagram but is implicit in f, so it is solved by trial or by chart.
A log–log chart of f against Re with curves of constant ε/D; it gives the turbulent friction factor by reading, not by solving.
Head loss along straight pipe due to wall friction, h_f = fLV²/(2gD), in metres of flowing fluid.
Head loss at a fitting, bend, valve or entrance, h_m = KV²/(2g); K is a dimensionless coefficient taken from tables for that fitting.
h = (V₁ − V₂)²/(2g) from Borda–Carnot, often written K = (1 − A₁/A₂)² based on the smaller-section velocity.
A plot of piezometric head p/(ρg) + z along the pipe; it lies one velocity head V²/(2g) below the total energy line.
A plot of total head H = p/(ρg) + z + V²/(2g); it drops by every head loss and rises across a pump.
Pipes joined end to end: the same discharge Q passes through each, and the total head loss is the sum of the individual losses.
Pipes branching and rejoining between the same two junctions: the head loss is the same in each branch and the discharges add.
One imaginary pipe that carries the same discharge with the same total head loss as the whole system; used to reduce networks to a single line.
The pressure wave set up when flow in a pipe is stopped or changed quickly; the Joukowsky rise is Δp = ρcV and the head rise is cV/g, where c is the wave speed in m/s.
A pipe that rises above the source free surface and delivers at a lower level; the driving head is the level difference and the crest works under sub-atmospheric pressure.

takeaways: Reynolds number decides the flow regime: low Re gives a straight dye thread, high Re gives a blurred cloud, and the change happens around 2000–4000.
Laminar pipe flow has a parabolic velocity profile, u_max = 2V, and the Hagen–Poiseuille result that discharge grows as D⁴ and falls as 1/μ.
The Darcy–Weisbach equation converts wall friction into a head loss proportional to f, L, V² and 1/D.
The friction factor is not a constant: it depends on Re in smooth pipes, on ε/D in fully rough pipes, and on both in between, which is what the Moody diagram shows.
Real systems lose head both along the pipe and at every entry, bend, valve and exit, so minor losses can dominate in short, crowded pipework.
The total energy line always falls in the direction of flow by the head loss, never rises except at a pump; the HGL sits one velocity head below it.
Series pipes share discharge and add head losses; parallel pipes share head loss and add discharges; either way the system reduces to one equivalent pipe.
Fast valve closure stores kinetic energy as a pressure wave, so the surge head cV/g can be many times the working head; a siphon works only while the crest pressure stays above vapour pressure.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to derive the Hagen–Poiseuille result from a force balance on a cylindrical element, apply Darcy–Weisbach with the Moody chart, tabulate minor-loss coefficients, and finish a pipe-network numerical answer with a clearly labelled HGL and TEL sketch.

bank.q: Describe the Reynolds experiment with a neat sketch. State what is observed as the velocity is slowly increased, define the Reynolds number, and give the critical values for pipe flow.
outline: Glass tube, dye reservoir, control valve, measuring tank arrangement
At low velocity the dye is a straight stable thread (laminar)
At higher velocity the thread wavers, then breaks into a cloud (transition, then turbulent)
Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν, with each symbol defined and units
Lower critical Re about 2000, upper about 4000; regime depends on Re, not on the fluid alone

bank.q: Derive the Hagen–Poiseuille equation for steady laminar flow in a circular pipe, starting from the forces on a cylindrical fluid element, and obtain the velocity profile and the relation between mean and maximum velocity.
outline: Assume steady, fully developed, laminar, incompressible, no slip at wall
Force balance: pressure force minus shear force equals zero on a cylinder of radius r
Newton's law of viscosity to relate shear stress to velocity gradient
Integrate with u = 0 at r = R to get the parabola u = (Δp/4μL)(R² − r²)
u_max at centre; integrate over area for Q = πΔpD⁴/(128μL)
Show u_max = 2V and wall shear stress τ₀ = ΔpD/(4L)

bank.q: Explain the Darcy–Weisbach equation for head loss in pipes. Show how the friction factor is related to wall shear stress and state what the friction factor depends on.
outline: h_f = fLV²/(2gD), each symbol and unit stated
Equating pressure drop with wall shear stress, τ₀ = fρV²/8
Fanning factor f′ and Darcy factor f, with f = 4f′
Dependence: Re in smooth pipes, ε/D in rough pipes, both in transition
Laminar case f = 64/Re, so h_f ∝ V

bank.q: Explain the Moody diagram. What is plotted against what, what are the three zones of the curve, and how is the friction factor read for a given pipe and discharge?
outline: Log–log plot of f against Re with ε/D as parameter
Laminar zone f = 64/Re, independent of roughness
Transition and smooth-pipe zone where f depends mainly on Re
Fully rough zone where curves flatten and f depends only on ε/D
Colebrook–White equation as the source of the curves; steps to read f and then find h_f

bank.q: List the major and minor losses of flow in pipes. Define the loss coefficient K and give typical values for a sharp entrance, a sudden enlargement, a 90° elbow and a fully open gate valve.
outline: Major loss from Darcy–Weisbach along straight pipe
Minor losses at entrance, exit, contraction, enlargement, bends, elbows, valves, fittings
h_m = KV²/(2g) with K defined and the velocity to be used stated
Typical values quoted as approximate ranges, not exact numbers
When minor losses can be neglected: long pipe, small K sum

bank.q: Explain the hydraulic gradient line and the total energy line for flow through a pipe. Sketch both for a reservoir feeding a pipe that discharges to atmosphere.
outline: Definitions of piezometric head p/(ρg) + z and total head plus V²/(2g)
TEL drawn at the reservoir surface and falling along the pipe
HGL one velocity head below TEL for uniform pipe
Entry loss and exit loss shown as sharp drops and rises in the plot
Rules: TEL never rises except at a pump; HGL can fall below the pipe if pressure goes negative

bank.q: Lubricating oil of dynamic viscosity 0.1 Pa·s and density 900 kg/m³ flows at 0.5 L/s through a 20 mm diameter, 30 m long pipe. Check that the flow is laminar, then find the pressure drop, the head loss in metres of oil and the centreline velocity.
outline: Convert Q to m³/s and find V = Q/A
Re = ρVD/μ, compare with 2000 and confirm laminar
Δp = 128μLQ/(πD⁴)
h_f = Δp/(ρg) in metres of oil
u_max = 2V; mention that wall shear stress follows from τ₀ = ΔpD/(4L)

bank.q: Water flows at 0.05 m³/s through a 200 mm diameter cast iron pipe 500 m long with f = 0.025. Find the velocity, the head loss by Darcy–Weisbach, the pressure drop, and the power needed to overcome friction.
outline: V = Q/A with area from diameter
h_f = fLV²/(2gD)
Δp = ρgh_f
Power = ρgQh_f in watts
Comment on whether minor losses would matter over this length

bank.q: A reservoir feeds a 150 mm pipe of length 200 m ending in a nozzle, through a sharp entrance, two 90° elbows and a gate valve. Taking f = 0.02 and suitable K values, find the discharge when the reservoir level is 15 m above the outlet.
outline: Apply Bernoulli between reservoir surface and jet, with head losses on the left
List each loss term: entry, friction, two elbows, valve, exit or jet velocity head
Express every loss in terms of V²/(2g)
Solve for V and then Q = AV
Iterate if f or K assumed; state assumptions

bank.q: Two pipes in series carry 0.03 m³/s. Pipe 1 is 300 mm diameter and 400 m long; pipe 2 is 200 mm diameter and 200 m long. Taking the same f = 0.02 for both, find the total head loss and the length of an equivalent 250 mm pipe.
outline: Same Q in both pipes, velocities from continuity
h_f for each pipe by Darcy–Weisbach, then add
Minor loss at the junction if asked
For the equivalent pipe, equate total head loss at the same Q
Solve for equivalent length (or diameter) from f L_e V_e²/(2gD_e)

bank.q: Two parallel pipes connect the same two reservoirs and together carry 0.08 m³/s. Pipe A is 200 mm diameter and 600 m long with f = 0.02; pipe B is 150 mm diameter and 600 m long with f = 0.024. Find the discharge in each pipe and the head loss between the junctions.
outline: Parallel rule: h_f is the same in both branches
Write h_f in terms of Q_A and Q_B using Q = AV
Continuity at the junction: Q_A + Q_B = total Q
Solve the resulting equation for one unknown, then the other
Compute h_f and check both branches give the same value

bank.q: Compare laminar and turbulent flow in pipes with respect to velocity profile, shear stress at the wall, friction factor and the way head loss varies with velocity. Explain why doubling the discharge has very different effects in the two regimes.
outline: Parabola versus flatter, fuller turbulent profile with a laminar sublayer
τ₀ from fρV²/8 in both, but f differs
Laminar f = 64/Re, so h_f ∝ V; turbulent f weakly dependent on Re, so h_f ≈ V^1.75 to V²
Use of the Moody chart to show the two regions
Practical consequence for pumping cost in a pipeline

bank.q: Explain water hammer in a pipe. Obtain the pressure rise for instantaneous closure, discuss the effect of closure time compared with 2L/c, and describe two methods of protecting a pipeline.
outline: Cause: kinetic energy of the moving column converted into elastic strain
Wave speed c = √(K/ρ) for a rigid pipe, corrected for pipe elasticity
Joukowsky rise Δp = ρcV and surge head cV/g
Slow closure: use the time of closure against 2L/c
Protection: surge tank, air vessel, slow-closing valve, bypass, stronger pipe

bank.q: A pumping main 2 km long and 300 mm diameter delivers water at 0.06 m³/s. Evaluate the share of major and minor losses, decide whether minor losses can be neglected, and recommend how the diameter choice affects running cost.
outline: Velocity from continuity, Re, then f from the Moody chart using an assumed ε
Major loss over 2 km by Darcy–Weisbach
Sum of minor losses with K values; compare the two as a percentage
Hagen–Poiseuille check only if the flow is laminar, which it will not be
D⁴ effect in laminar flow, D⁵ effect on head loss for fixed Q in turbulent flow
Conclusion on capital cost versus pumping power, plus a sketch of TEL and HGL with the pump rise

glossary.def: The property μ, in Pa·s, that measures a fluid's resistance to shear, equal to shear stress divided by velocity gradient.
ν = μ/ρ in m²/s, the dynamic viscosity divided by density.
A fluid in which shear stress is directly proportional to velocity gradient, so μ is constant at a given temperature.
The rule that fluid in contact with a solid surface has the same velocity as the surface, so velocity is zero at a fixed pipe wall.
Tangential force per unit area, in Pa, acting between fluid layers or between fluid and wall.
The volume of fluid passing a section per unit time, Q = AV, in m³/s.
The discharge divided by the cross-sectional area, V = Q/A, in m/s.
The term V²/(2g) in metres, the height to which the kinetic energy of the flow could lift the fluid.
p/(ρg) + z, in metres, the sum of pressure head and elevation head at a section.
The energy per unit weight, in metres of flowing fluid, lost to friction and fittings between two sections.
The shear stress at the pipe wall, τ₀ = fρV²/8, which balances the pressure force in fully developed flow.
The head loss per unit length, i = h_f/L, dimensionless.
The equivalent sand-grain height ε, in metres, representing the size of wall irregularities in turbulent flow.
The very thin layer of laminar-flowing fluid next to a wall in turbulent flow; roughness smaller than it does not affect f.
A rotating pocket of fluid in turbulent flow that carries momentum across streamlines and increases mixing.
Formation and violent collapse of vapour bubbles when local pressure falls below the vapour pressure, damaging the pipe or impeller.
Filling a siphon or pump with liquid and removing air so that the pressure difference can act on a continuous liquid column.
The large pipe that carries water from a reservoir or surge tank down to a hydro turbine.
An open or closed tank on a pipeline that absorbs the pressure wave of water hammer.
Pressure fluctuation in a pipe caused by a rapid change of flow velocity.
A pipe or duct that lifts liquid above its source level and discharges it at a lower level, driven by the head difference.
The Reynolds number band, roughly 2000 to 4000, where the flow alternates between laminar and turbulent.
